Battle on the Ice: Russia. The Battle on the Ice, also known as the Battle of Lake Peipus, took place on 5 April 1242.

Heian period: Japan. The Heian period (平安時代, Heian jidai) is the last division of classical Japanese history, running from 794 to 1185.
In which country is Socialism with Chinese characteristics based?

History of Massachusetts: United States. The area that is now Massachusetts was colonized by English settlers in the early 17th century and became the Commonwealth of Massachusetts in the 18th century.

Battle of Passchendaele: Belgium. Passchendaele (now Passendale) lies on the last ridge east of Ypres, 5 mi (8 km) from Roulers (now Roeselare), a junction of the Bruges-(Brugge)-to-Kortrijk railway.
In which country was the French Second Republic?
French Second Republic: France. The republic existed from 1848, when the monarchy fell, until its dissolution only four years later in 1852 upon the proclamation of the Second French Empire.

Han dynasty: Chinese Empire. It was succeeded by the Three Kingdoms period (220–280 AD) and also briefly interrupted by the Xin dynasty (9–23 AD) established by the usurping regent Wang Mang.

Liberal Democrats (UK): United Kingdom. The Liberal Democrats, colloquially known as the Lib Dems, is a political party in the United Kingdom.
Which of these is an official language of Ahmadiyya?
Ahmadiyya: Urdu. Adherents of the Ahmadiyya—a term adopted expressly in reference to Muhammad's alternative name Ahmad—are known as Ahmadi Muslims or simply Ahmadis.

Goryeo: Korean. Throughout its existence, Goryeo, alongside Unified Silla, was known to be the Golden Age of Buddhism in Korea.

Sasanian Empire: Middle Persian. It also helped shape European and Asian medieval art.
Which country uses the Reichsmark as its official currency?
The Reichsmark is the official currency of Nazi Germany. After Hitler was appointed Chancellor of Germany in 1933, the Nazi Party began to eliminate political opposition and consolidate power.

The son of an Irish mother and an Italian Civil War veteran, this Lower East Side native served four terms as New York's governor before becoming his party's 1928 presidential nominee — losing in a landslide to Herbert Hoover. Who was he?
Al Smith (December 30, 1873 - October 4, 1944) was an American politician who served as the 42nd governor of New York from 1919 to 1920 and again from 1923 to 1928.

This political theory leans heavily on the "non-aggression principle" to argue that even policing, courts, and defense could be supplied by private providers in a wholly voluntary society. What's this stateless ideology called?

Anarcho-capitalism (colloquially: ANCAP, Ancap, AnCap, or An-Cap) is a political ideology and economic theory that advocates for the abolition of state monopolies and promotes their replacement with private providers.

Convicted as a war criminal for his role in the deportation of Dutch Jews while serving as Reichskommissar of the Netherlands, this man had briefly been Austria's chancellor before the 1938 Anschluss — who was he?

Arthur Seyss-Inquart (Austrian German; 22 July 1892 - 16 October 1946) was an Austrian Nazi politician and convicted war criminal who served as Chancellor of Austria in 1938 for two days before the Anschluss.

Fought on September 19, 1356, during the Hundred Years' War, this clash saw Edward the Black Prince and 6,000 Anglo-Gascons defend a fortified position against 14,000 to 16,000 French attackers. Name it.
Battle of Poitiers was fought on 19 September 1356, during the Hundred Years' War, between a French army commanded by King John II and an Anglo-Gascon force under Edward, the Black Prince.
Born in the Quebec city of Baie-Comeau and once a prominent labour lawyer, he led the Progressive Conservatives to become Canada's 18th prime minister in 1984 — who was he?
Brian Mulroney (March 20, 1939 - February 29, 2024) was a Canadian lawyer, businessman, and politician who served as the 18th prime minister of Canada from 1984 to 1993.

The U.S. Navy's leading submarine authority, this fleet admiral commanded Allied forces across the Pacific during World War II and later helped win approval to build the first nuclear-powered submarine — who is he?
Chester W. Nimitz (24 February 1885 - 20 February 1966) was a fleet admiral in the United States Navy.
This American politician served as the 44th vice president under George H. W. Bush, after representing Indiana in both houses of Congress — who is he?

Dan Quayle (born February 4, 1947) is an American retired politician and Indiana National Guard veteran who served as the 44th vice president of the United States from 1989 to 1993 under President George H. W. Bush.

A retired U.S. Army colonel who led an early tank battle in the Gulf War and helped plan the 1999 NATO bombing of Yugoslavia, this officer later wrote a 1997 book arguing for radical Army reform. Who is he?
Douglas Macgregor (born January 4, 1947) is a retired colonel in the United States Army, former government official, author, consultant, and political commentator.
Closely aligned with Joseph Stalin's Soviet Union, this German communist leader died in 1944 after leading his party's opposition to the Weimar Republic in its final years — who is he?
Ernst Thälmann (16 April 1886 - 18 August 1944) was a German communist politician, revolutionary, and leader of the Communist Party of Germany (KPD) from 1925 to 1933.
He began on the Catholic nationalist right and served under Vichy before moving left to become the first left-wing president of France's Fifth Republic — and its longest-serving. Who was he?
François Mitterrand (26 October 1916 - 8 January 1996) was President of France from 1981 to 1995.

In November 1688 the Catholic King James II was deposed in favor of his daughter Mary II and her Dutch husband William of Orange — an event some historians call the last successful invasion of England. What is it called?

Glorious Revolution was the deposition of King James II in November 1688. The two ruled as joint monarchs of England, Scotland, and Ireland until Mary's death in 1694, when William became ruler in his own right.

Commissioned into a light horse unit his own father raised, he became the first Australian to reach lieutenant general and led the Desert Mounted Corps to one of military history's fastest pursuits. Who was this WWI commander?

Harry Chauvel (16 April 1865 - 4 March 1945) was a senior officer of the Australian Imperial Force who fought at Gallipoli and during the Sinai and Palestine Campaign in the Middle Eastern theatre of the First World War.
Formed in 1942 from earlier Polish resistance cells, this underground force became one of WWII Europe's largest, fighting German occupiers under London-exiled leadership — which organization?
Home Army (abbreviated AK) was the dominant resistance movement in German-occupied Poland during World War II.
The son of Abraham and Sarah and father of Jacob and Esau, this patriarch's name means 'he will laugh,' referencing his parents' reaction to news of his birth at their advanced ages — who is he?
Isaac is the second Hebrew patriarch in Judaism and an important figure in the Abrahamic religions, including Samaritanism, Christianity, Islam, the Bah' Faith, and Rastafari.
Whose decades campaigning on immigration and "traditional values" so shifted French debate that it spawned a coined term for the "-isation of minds" — the founder of the National Front?
Jean-Marie Le Pen (20 June 1928 - 7 January 2025) was a French politician who founded the far-right National Front (now National Rally) party.

Starting in 1950 this Wisconsin senator became the public face of Cold War fears, alleging communists had infiltrated the government, universities, and Hollywood — until the Senate censured him in 1954. Who was he?
Joseph McCarthy (November 14, 1908 - May 2, 1957) was an American politician who served as a Republican senator from Wisconsin from 1947 until his death in 1957.
Representing a Berlin district in the Bundestag, this politician chaired the SPD's youth organization before rising to General Secretary of the party — who is he?
Kevin Kühnert (born 1 July 1989) is a German politician of Social Democratic Party (SPD) who served as member of the Bundestag from 2021 to 2025, representing Berlin-Tempelhof-Schneberg.
Fueled in part by the country's religious mosaic of Christians, Sunnis, Shias, and Druze, which 1975–1990 conflict killed an estimated 150,000 and drove nearly a million people into exile?
Lebanese Civil War was a multifaceted armed conflict that took place from 1975 to 1990.
He served as Senegal's prime minister from 2004 to 2007 before a falling-out with his mentor led him to found a new party and later win the presidency in 2012 — who is he?
Macky Sall (French; born 11 December 1961) is a Senegalese politician who served as the fourth president of Senegal from 2012 to 2024.
In a memorable episode, this Pakistani chief minister's own Wikipedia page was cited by the Attorney General as proof of her academic credentials — who is she?
Maryam Nawaz (born 28 October 1973) is a Pakistani politician who has served as the 19th chief minister of Punjab since 26 February 2024.
A 1991 graduate of an elite airborne academy, this Ukrainian-born officer has led Russia's paratrooper forces since 2022 - who is he?
Mikhail Teplinsky (born 9 January 1969) is a Ukrainian-born Russian military officer who has served as commander of the Russian Airborne Forces since 2022.
The 126th holder of his throne and a one-time history student at Oxford, he became emperor in 2019 when his father Akihito abdicated — who is he?
Naruhito (born 23 February 1960) is Emperor of Japan.

Known as the 'Demon Daimyo,' this Japanese samurai and warlord is regarded as the first 'Great Unifier' of Japan during the Sengoku period, alongside retainers Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu — who is he?
Oda Nobunaga (23 June 1534 - 21 June 1582) was a Japanese samurai and daimy and one of the leading figures of the Sengoku and Azuchi-Momoyama periods.
A silversmith from Boston's North End, this American rode at midnight in 1775 to warn militia of British troops marching toward Lexington and Concord. Who is this?
Paul Revere was American silversmith and military officer (1735–1818).
Suspended in a soybean-oil and lecithin emulsion that gives it a milky white color, this intravenous anesthetic is prized for quick recovery — what is it?
Propofol is the active component of an intravenous anesthetic used for induction and maintenance of general anesthesia.
A former Navy veteran and healthcare executive, he served two terms as Florida's governor before becoming the state's senior U.S. senator in 2019 — who is he?
Rick Scott (n Myers; born December 1, 1952) is an American attorney, businessman, politician, and Navy veteran serving as the senior United States senator from Florida, a seat he has held since 2019.
As students in 1930s Paris, he and Michel Aflaq blended nationalism and socialism into a doctrine, then co-founded the Ba'ath Party — and he was later assassinated in Paris in 1980. Who was he?
Salah al-Din al-Bitar (1 January 1912 - 21 July 1980) was a Syrian politician who co-founded the Baath Party with Michel Aflaq in the early 1940s.
After a 2022 split in a Maharashtra party, this faction led by former chief minister Uddhav Thackeray received a new 'Flaming Torch' symbol from India's Election Commission — which faction?
Shiv Sena (UBT) (Uddhav Balasaheb Thackeray) is a Hindutva-based, Marathi regionalist, nationalist political party formed in 2022.
Now leading an alternate government from exile in Lithuania and Poland, this Belarusian opposition figure stepped into the 2020 presidential race after her husband's arrest — who is she?
Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya (ne Pilipchuk; born 11 September 1982) is a Belarusian opposition leader and political activist.

This Japanese term describes marginalized, sometimes homeless young people who gather in the alleys around Tokyo's Shinjuku Toho Building — many of them runaways seeking a sense of community after experiencing bullying — what's the term?
Toyoko kids is a Japanese term describing marginalized youth, including some homeless, who gather in the back alleys around the Shinjuku Toho Building in Kabukicho.
This Russian right-wing populist politician led a nationalist party from its 1992 founding until his death in 2022, twice serving as deputy chairman of the State Duma. Who is he?

Vladimir Zhirinovsky (25 April 1946 - 6 April 2022) was a Russian right-wing populist politician who served as the leader of the Liberal Democratic Party of Russia (LDPR) from its creation in 1992 until his death in 2022.

This 2023 musical fantasy directed by Paul King stars Timothée Chalamet and serves as a prequel to the 1971 film, portraying the protagonist's early days as a chocolatier. What is this film adaptation based on Roald Dahl's novel called?
Wonka (film) is a 2023 musical fantasy film directed by Paul King, who co-wrote the screenplay with Simon Farnaby.

1984 anti-Sikh riots: Series of organised pogroms in India.

Augusto Pinochet: Dictator of Chile from 1973 to 1990.

Battle of Mogadishu (1993): Military conflict during the Somali Civil War.
Born Warren Wilhelm Jr., this Democratic politician served as New York City's public advocate before becoming its 110th mayor and describing economic inequality as a 'tale of two cities' — who is he?
Bill de Blasio: Mayor of New York City from 2014 to 2021.

Charan Singh: Prime Minister of India from 1979 to 1980. Singh was principally known for his land and agricultural reform initiatives, and was Member of Parliament (MP) for Baghpat.
Considered by some the greatest lawyer of the 20th century, this ACLU leader argued the Leopold and Loeb case and the Scopes 'monkey' trial — who is he?
Clarence Darrow: American lawyer and politician (1857–1938)
Rising from Persis to topple the Median Empire, this ruler founded the Achaemenid dynasty and built what became, in its day, the largest empire the world had yet seen — who was he?
Cyrus the Great: Founder of the Achaemenid Empire. Cyrus II of Persia (c. 600 – 530 BC), commonly known as Cyrus the Great, was the founder of the Achaemenid Empire.
Dubbed the "Architect of Modern China," this Sichuan-born leader steered the nation toward a socialist market economy after Mao's death — who was he?
Deng Xiaoping: Leader of China from 1978 to 1989.

Earl Warren: Chief Justice of the United States from 1953 to 1969.

Eva Perón: First Lady of Argentina from 1946 to 1952.

First Sino-Japanese War: 1894–1895 war between China and Japan.
The first female student at Abeokuta Grammar School, this Nigerian educator and women's-rights organizer wove together anti-imperialist, Pan-Africanist, and feminist ideals — who is she?
The eldest son of former Indonesian president Joko Widodo, this politician became vice president in 2024 as running mate to Prabowo Subianto after serving as mayor of Surakarta — who is he?
Gibran Rakabuming Raka: Vice President of Indonesia since 2024.
After his father was executed in the Stockholm Bloodbath, he led a war of liberation and was elected king in 1523 — the day Sweden left the Kalmar Union and now its National Day. Which Swedish king?
Gustav Vasa: King of Sweden from 1523 to 1560.
He was Iran's top negotiator with the EU three before becoming the country's seventh president in 2013 — which sharia-lawyer-turned-cleric served until 2021?
Hassan Rouhani: President of Iran from 2013 to 2021. Hassan Rouhani (born Hassan Fereydoun, 12 November 1948) is an Iranian politician who served as the seventh president of Iran from 2013 to 2021.
Spanning roughly 1000 to 1300 CE, this European era saw a population boom, the 12th-century renaissance, and the growth of cities before the Black Death struck — which period?
High Middle Ages: Period of European history between AD 1000 and 1350.

It runs from our species' emergence in Africa some 300,000 years ago, through the great migration out during the last Ice Age, to the Neolithic farms and earliest writing systems — what sweeping subject is this?
Human history: Records of Earth's people.
A conflict from 1922 to 1923 following Irish independence, fought between the Provisional Government of Ireland and the Anti-Treaty IRA over the Anglo-Irish Treaty. What is this?

Irish Civil War: 1922–1923 conflict between factions of the IRA. The National Army benefited from substantial quantities of weapons provided by the British government, particularly artillery and armoured cars.
The only sitting member of the U.S. House ever elected president, this 20th commander-in-chief died in 1881 after being shot just months into office — who is he?
James A. Garfield: President of the United States in 1881.
A protégé of Martin Luther King Jr., this Baptist minister and civil rights leader founded the organizations that merged into the Rainbow/PUSH Coalition — who is he?
Jesse Jackson: American minister, activist and politician (1941–2026)
One of the richest men of his era, this fourth son of Edward III took his name from the Flemish city of his birth and founded the royal House of Lancaster; who was he?
John of Gaunt: English prince and regent (1340–1399)
Roman emperor from 527 to 565, his dream of restoring the empire saw his general Belisarius reclaim North Africa, Italy and Rome from the Ostrogoths — who was he?
Justinian I: Roman emperor from 527 to 565. The praetorian prefect Liberius reclaimed the south of the Iberian Peninsula, establishing the province of Spania.
This 7th-century Arab horseman first fought against Muhammad for the Quraysh, then converted and led Muslim armies through Iraq and Syria — who was he?
Khalid ibn al-Walid: Arab Muslim general (died 642)
Assassinated by the SS during the Night of the Long Knives in 1934, this German officer had served as the second-to-last chancellor of the Weimar Republic — who was he?
Kurt von Schleicher: Chancellor of Germany from 1932 to 1933.

A former aide to Herbert Hoover turned investment banker, he became an original member and later chairman of the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission and a major figure in postwar nuclear policy — who was he?
He quit school after second grade, didn't read until age ten, and went from metalworker and union firebrand to president of Brazil — who is it?
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva: President of Brazil (2003–2011; since 2023)
A sepoy in the Bengal Native Infantry who died in April 1857, this soldier's actions helped spark the rebellion that ended East India Company rule and ushered in the British Raj — who is he?
Mangal Pandey: Indian soldier and freedom fighter (1827–1857)
Imprisoned by Israel since 2002 on charges tied to deadly attacks he denies involvement in, this Palestinian legislator has long championed a two-state solution — who is he?
Married to the heir apparent of a Scandinavian throne, this royal underwent a lung transplant in 2026 after a diagnosis of pulmonary fibrosis — who is she?
Princess Beatrice of the United Kingdom
Mette-Marit, Crown Princess of Norway: Norwegian royal (born 1973)

Historians generally date this current period of human history from around 1500, though many now reserve its label for events from the 19th century onward, like the Industrial Revolution — what span of time is this?
Modern era: Current period of history. Since the 1990s, it has been more common among historians to refer to the period after the Middle Ages and up to the 19th century as the early modern period.
Son of Mehmed III and Halime Sultan, this Ottoman ruler held the throne twice, briefly in 1617–1618 and again in 1622–1623 — who was he?
Mustafa I: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire (r. 1617–1618, 1622–1623)
Widely seen as ill-prepared to rule a vast empire, he was the last monarch to reign before the Russian Revolution and led his country into World War I — which emperor?
Nicholas II: Emperor of Russia from 1894 to 1917.
This four-star general commanded the defense of Kyiv and led the 2022 Kharkiv counteroffensive before becoming commander-in-chief of Ukraine's armed forces in 2024 — who is he?
This historical region of northeastern Greater Iran became the political and cultural base of the Parni people and the Arsacid dynasty — lending its name to a famous empire. Which region?

Parthia: Historical region located in northeastern Iran. Parthia (Old Persian: 𐎱𐎼𐎰𐎺 Parθava; Parthian: 𐭐𐭓𐭕𐭅 Parθaw; Middle Persian: 𐭯𐭫𐭮𐭥𐭡𐭥 Pahlaw) is a historical region located in northeastern Greater Iran.

Its name comes from Ancient Greek for "love of wisdom," and once upon a time physics and psychology were considered branches of it before going their separate academic ways. What rational, critical field is this?
Philosophy: Study of general and fundamental questions.
This Macedonian Greek general, one of Alexander the Great's most trusted companions, retrieved his leader's body after his death and founded a new ruling dynasty in Egypt — who is he?
Ptolemy I Soter: Pharaoh of Egypt from 305 to 282 BC.
This Cuban revolutionary succeeded his brother as president in 2008 and served as the country's defense minister for nearly five decades — who is he?
Raúl Castro: President of Cuba from 2008 to 2018.
Abrasive and reactionary, this right-wing populist and economic nationalist served as New Zealand's 31st prime minister from 1975 to 1984 — who was he?
Robert Muldoon: Prime Minister of New Zealand from 1975 to 1984. After a troubled childhood, Muldoon served as a corporal and sergeant in the army in the Second World War.

On a single 1929 day in a Chicago garage, seven men were lined against a wall and gunned down — some of the killers disguised as police — in a brutal flashpoint of Prohibition-era gang warfare. What is this killing known as?

Saint Valentine's Day Massacre: 1929 gang shooting in Chicago. The Saint Valentine's Day Massacre was the murder of seven members and associates of Chicago's North Side Gang on Saint Valentine's Day 1929.

This wave of mass production, standardization, and rapid scientific discovery, sometimes dubbed the Technological era, is generally dated between 1870 and the outbreak of World War I in 1914. What period was this?
Second Industrial Revolution: 1870–1914 electrical and chemical era.
A writer who governed Tokyo from 1999 to 2012, this prominent ultranationalist was widely criticized for xenophobic and racist remarks against Chinese and Koreans in Japan — who was he?
Across religions this immortal, immaterial essence goes by many names — atman in Hinduism, jiva in Jainism, ruh in Islam — but what's its common English term?
Soul: In religion and philosophy, immaterial essence of a living being.
A London School of Economics graduate from a wealthy family, he led Togo from its 1958 election to independence as prime minister and then president, until his 1963 assassination — who was he?

Sylvanus Olympio: President of Togo from 1960 to 1963. After World War II, Olympio became prominent in efforts for independence of Togo and his party won the 1958 election, making him the prime minister of the country.
Founded by Aleister Crowley in the early 1900s, this occult philosophy centers on discovering one's 'True Will' and the maxim 'Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the Law' — what is it?
Thelema: New religious movement founded by Aleister Crowley.
This Haitian general rose from a slave rebellion to become Governor-General-for-life of Saint-Domingue before ultimately clashing with Napoleon's troops. Who was he?
Toussaint Louverture: Haitian general and revolutionary (1744–1803)
Composed in an archaic Sanskrit dialect, this collection of four ancient hymn texts forms the oldest layer of Hindu scripture — what are they collectively called?

Wang Jian (Qin): 3rd century BC Chinese military general.
Known as "Bill," this British field marshal led the so-called "forgotten army" in the Burma campaign before later serving as governor-general of Australia — who was he?
William Slim, 1st Viscount Slim: British Army field marshal, Governor-General of Australia, and author (1891–1970)

This Israeli politician served as defense minister from 2022 until his dismissal by the prime minister in November 2024, having earlier held posts including construction, immigration, and education minister after starting out in the navy. Who is he?
Yoav Gallant: Israeli politician & military officer (born 1958)
Who wrote Universal Declaration of Human Rights?

Universal Declaration of Human Rights → United Nations General Assembly. All 193 member states of the UN have ratified at least one of the nine binding treaties influenced by the Declaration, with the vast majority ratifying four or more.

Four novels and fifty-six short stories about a certain consulting detective made his name — but this knighted British writer-physician also invented Professor Challenger. Who was he?
Arthur Conan Doyle (22 May 1859 - 7 July 1930) was a British writer and physician.
The first production aircraft of its type, this American military transport combines vertical takeoff and landing with long-range cruise performance—what is it?
Bell Boeing V-22 Osprey is an American multi-use, tiltrotor military transport and cargo aircraft with both vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) and short takeoff and landing (STOL) capabilities.
Element 107, a synthetic transactinide whose most stable known isotope lasts barely 2.4 minutes, takes its name from a famous Danish physicist — what is it?
Bohrium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Bh and atomic number 107.

C Sharp (programming language) is a general-purpose high-level programming language supporting multiple paradigms.
This clouding of the eye's lens is responsible for nearly 40 percent of blindness cases worldwide, often causing halos around lights and trouble seeing at night — what condition is it?
Cataract is a cloudy area in the lens of the eye that impairs vision.
Linked to repeated head trauma, this worsening neurodegenerative disease turns up in boxers and footballers — and even in soccer players, largely from heading the ball. What is it?

Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is a neurodegenerative disease linked to repeated trauma to the head. The encephalopathy symptoms can include behavioral problems, mood problems, and problems with thinking.
This group of mostly evergreen, cone-bearing trees and shrubs reproduces via wind-pollination, with the seeds themselves also scattered by the wind — what plant group is it?
Conifer are a group of vascular plants and a subset of gymnosperms.
A law professor known for scholarship on retribution and criminal sentencing, this Harvard-trained academic was killed in 2014 in a murder-for-hire scheme linked to a custody dispute — who is he?

Dan Markel (October 9, 1972 - July 19, 2014) was a Canadian-born attorney and law professor who wrote various works on retribution in criminal law and sentencing with a focus on the role of punishment in the criminal justice system.
A member of the catecholamine family made by stripping a carboxyl group from L-DOPA, this brain chemical is central to reward-motivated behavior — what is it?
Dopamine (DA, a contraction of 3,4-dihydroxyphenethylamine) is a neuromodulatory molecule that plays several important roles in cells.
In this lung disease, the walls between tiny air sacs break down into fewer, larger spaces, shrinking the surface available for gas exchange and starving the blood of oxygen. What condition?
Emphysema is a condition of the lung marked by abnormal enlargement of the alveoli with loss of pulmonary elasticity.
Despite its name, this highly sociable oceanic dolphin earned its label from a skull resembling the orca's — it can reach 20 feet and even forms mixed pods with bottlenose dolphins. What is it?
False killer whale (Pseudorca crassidens) is a species of oceanic dolphin that is the only extant representative of the genus Pseudorca.
Having led Renault, Sauber, and Alfa Romeo's F1 outfits, this French engineer took the reins at Ferrari as team principal in 2023 — who is he?
Fred Vasseur (French; born 28 May 1968) is a French motorsport executive, businessman and engineer.

This metabolic pathway builds glucose from non-carbohydrate sources, occurring mainly in the liver in vertebrates, and serves as one of the body's two main tools for maintaining blood sugar — what process is it?
Gluconeogenesis (GNG) is a metabolic pathway that results in the biosynthesis of glucose from certain non-carbohydrate carbon substrates.
Newborns with this severe genetic skin disorder are born encased in thick, diamond-shaped plates separated by deep cracks that restrict movement and breathing — what is it?
Harlequin-type ichthyosis is a genetic disorder that results in thickened skin over nearly the entire body at birth.

Which field of study leans on anthropology, paleontology, and genetics to trace how our ancestors gradually picked up bipedalism, dexterity, and complex language — a story that turned out to be weblike rather than a tidy straight line?
Human evolution is a distinct species of the hominid family of primates, which includes all the great apes.
Denoted by the symbol ∞, this concept of the boundless and endless has been debated by philosophers since ancient Greece and by mathematicians since the 17th century — what is it?
Infinity is something which is boundless, limitless, or endless.
This British chemical engineer founded and leads a global chemicals conglomerate in 1998, and was briefly the richest person in the UK before shifting his tax residence to Monaco. Who is he?
Jim Ratcliffe (born 18 October 1952) is a British billionaire, chemical engineer, and businessman.
Her women's absolute land speed record stood until 2019, she got her own action figure, and Google honored her with a Doodle in 2023 — this deaf stuntwoman and racer. Who is she?
Kitty O'Neil ((1946-03-24)March 24, 1946 - (2018-11-02)November 2, 2018) was an American stuntwoman and auto-racer, often called "the fastest woman in the world" for her various speed records.
This Chinese herbalist, martial artist, and tactical advisor died in 1933 claiming a birth year of 1677 — a longevity claim gerontologists now regard as myth — who was he?
Li Ching-Yuen (simplified; traditional; pinyin: L Qngyn, died 6 May 1933) was a Chinese herbalist, martial artist and tactical advisor, known for his supposed extreme longevity.
Caused by a compromised lymphatic system, this condition raises infection risk in affected tissue and is treated with compression and massage rather than water pills — what is it?
Lymphedema (USA), lymphoedema (UK) also known as lymphatic edema (US)/oedema (UK), is a condition of localized swelling caused by a compromised lymphatic system.
This German-British theoretical physicist won a Nobel Prize for his statistical interpretation of the wavefunction, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics. Who is he?
Max Born (11 December 1882 - 5 January 1970) was a German-British theoretical physicist who was instrumental in the development of quantum mechanics.
This dark-coated member of the weasel family comes in American and European species, plus an extinct 'sea' relative — what animal is it?

Mink are dark-coloured, semiaquatic, carnivorous mammals in the genera Mustela and Neogale and part of the family Mustelidae, which also includes weasels, stoats, martens, otters, badgers, and others.
Developed under a hypersonic flight program in the late 1990s, three single-use examples of this scramjet aircraft were built, the first destroyed in a 2001 test flight — which record holder is it?
NASA X-43 was an experimental unmanned hypersonic aircraft with multiple planned scale variations meant to test various aspects of hypersonic flight.
The smallest of its type, this Canadian gun dog has webbed feet and lures waterfowl to shore with playful antics before fetching them from the water — which breed is it?
Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever is a medium-sized gun dog bred primarily for hunting.

Created by Danish-Canadian programmer Rasmus Lerdorf in 1993 and released in 1995, this general-purpose scripting language was originally short for 'Personal Home Page' before becoming a recursive backronym — name the language?
PHP is a general-purpose scripting language geared towards web development.
This class of compounds is defined by a direct single bond between two oxygen atoms, denoted R−O−O−R — what are they called?
Peroxide are a group of molecules with the structure ROOR, where each R represents a radical (a portion of a complete molecule; not a free radical) and the O's are single oxygen atoms.
Its common name is shared with an unrelated tropical fruit, but this genus of roughly 200 herbaceous species — also called fleaworts — belongs to the family Plantaginaceae. Which genus?
Plantago is a genus of about 200 species of flowering plants in the family Plantaginaceae, commonly called plantains or fleaworts.
This sense of self-movement, force, and body position is mediated by receptors located within muscles, tendons, and joints — what is it called?
Proprioception (--) is the sense of self-movement, force, and body position. Proprioception ( PROH-pree-oh-SEP-shən, -⁠ə-) is the sense of self-movement, force, and body position.
Distinguished from its smaller relative the crow mainly by size, this large-bodied passerine bird genus includes the common and thick-billed species, the biggest passerines alive — what bird is it?
Raven is any of several large-bodied passerine bird species in the genus Corvus.
Created by Yukihiro 'Matz' Matsumoto in 1990s Japan, this dynamically typed programming language treats absolutely everything — even primitive data types — as an object — what's the language?
Ruby (programming language) is a general-purpose programming language designed with an emphasis on programming productivity and simplicity.
Made by Novo Nordisk and taken by injection or pill, this peptide medicine doubles as a diabetes treatment and a weight-management drug — what is it?
Semaglutide is an anti-diabetic medication used for the treatment of type 2 diabetes, and an anti-obesity medication used for weight management.

With the formula NaNO3 and historically mined in massive deposits in Chile, this white, deliquescent salt is a key industrial source used to make fertilizers, pyrotechnics, and explosives — which compound?
Sodium nitrate is the chemical compound with the formula NaNO3. The mineral form is also known as nitratine, nitratite or soda niter.
A Jamaican-British Marxist sociologist who co-founded New Left Review, this thinker became a founding figure of the Birmingham School of Cultural Studies — who was he?
Stuart Hall (cultural theorist) (3 February 1932 - 10 February 2014) was a Jamaican-British Marxist sociologist, cultural theorist, and political activist.
Caused by Clostridium tetani, this infection brings on recurring muscle spasms that can last weeks and prove fatal in about 10% of cases — what is it commonly known as?
Tetanus (from Ancient Greek 'tension', 'stretched', 'rigid'), also known as lockjaw, is a bacterial infection caused by Clostridium tetani and characterized by muscle spasms.
Roughly eight times more potent than an older analogue, this bleeding-control medication is also prescribed for hereditary angioedema — what is it?
Tranexamic acid is a medication used to treat or prevent excessive blood loss from major trauma, postpartum bleeding, surgery, tooth removal, nosebleeds, and heavy menstruation.
This British-American structural biologist shared the 2009 Nobel in Chemistry for revealing the ribosome's structure and later led the Royal Society as president — who is he?
Venki Ramakrishnan (born 1952) is a British-American structural biologist.
This biological process unfolds in predictable phases — hemostasis, inflammation, cell proliferation, and tissue remodeling — to replace damaged skin after the barrier is broken. What is it?
Wound healing refers to a living organism's replacement of destroyed or damaged tissue by newly produced tissue.

Alan Greenspan: American economist and financial advisor (born 1926)

This American anthropologist studied women's weaving and blacksmithing work in Indonesia and later designed microcredit programs to fight rural poverty — who was she?
Known commonly as palms, this family of over 2,600 flowering plant species includes climbers, shrubs, and tree-like forms mostly found in the tropics — what's the family called?
Arecaceae: Palm family of flowering plants.

Australopithecus: Genus of hominin ancestral to modern humans. The genera Homo (which includes modern humans), Paranthropus, and Kenyanthropus evolved from some Australopithecus species.
This inflammatory condition causes recurring, painful mouth sores along with eye inflammation and arthritis, and is diagnosed after at least three sore outbreaks in a year — which condition?
Behçet's disease: Inflammatory disorder. Behçet's disease or Behçet's syndrome (BD; sometimes written Behcet) is a type of inflammatory disorder which affects multiple parts of the body.
This medium-sized antelope of India and Nepal sports corkscrew horns up to 30 inches long and a striking two-tone coat, with white around the eyes set against black face stripes — which animal?
Blackbuck: Antelope native to India and Nepal. The blackbuck (Antilope cervicapra), also known as the Indian antelope, is a medium-sized antelope native to India and Nepal.
Nicknamed 'murderer's thumb' or 'stubbed thumb,' this genetic trait gives about 2% of people a short, rounded thumb linked to the HOXD13 gene — what is it?
Brachydactyly type D: Abnormal shortening of the distal part of the thumb.
A cole crop related to broccoli, cauliflower and Brussels sprouts, the heaviest recorded head of this leafy vegetable weighed nearly 138 pounds — what is it?
Cabbage: Leafy vegetable in the flowering plant family Brassicaceae.

Cerebrum: Large part of the brain containing the cerebral cortex.
This Dutch scientist discovered Saturn's largest moon and invented the pendulum clock, the most accurate timekeeper for nearly three centuries — who is he?

Cynodon dactylon: Species of grass. Cynodon dactylon, commonly known as Bermuda grass or as couch grass in Australia and New Zealand, is a grass found worldwide in warm and tropical climates.
This central nervous system stimulant is the 'right-handed' mirror-image form of a well-known molecule, prescribed for ADHD and narcolepsy and sometimes given as an inactive prodrug — what is it?
Dextroamphetamine: CNS stimulant and isomer of amphetamine.
A broad-spectrum member of the tetracycline class, this antibiotic treats everything from acne and chlamydia to Lyme disease and cholera — though it'll make you sunburn more easily. Which drug?
Doxycycline: Tetracycline-class antibiotic. It is used to treat bacterial pneumonia, acne, chlamydia infections, Lyme disease, cholera, typhus, and syphilis, and is sometimes used to prevent malaria.
Despite its name, this South American freshwater fish is actually a knifefish, not a true eel, and produces powerful discharges using specialized tissue — which species?
Electrophorus electricus: South American electric fish. It is considered as a freshwater teleost which contains an electrogenic tissue that produces electric discharges.
This flowering shrub in the family Erythroxylaceae is one of only two species whose leaves are cultivated to produce a notorious stimulant — which plant is it?
Erythroxylum coca: Species of flowering plant.
Sporting an orange-red breast rimmed in grey and brown upperparts, this small insect-eating songbird ranges from Western Siberia to North Africa — which bird?
European robin: Species of bird. It is found across Europe, as far east as Western Siberia, and as far south as North Africa.
This genus of over 200 stinging insect species, Solenopsis, includes 'ginger' and 'tropical' varieties named for their painful bite and reddish coloring — what are they commonly called?
Fire ant: Genus of red ants.
Often bonded to glucose to form sucrose, this simple sugar is found in honey, fruit, and most root vegetables — which sugar?
Fructose: Simple ketonic monosaccharide found in many plants.

Gharial: Crocodilian native to the Indian subcontinent.
The seeds of five plants in this family, including rice, wheat, maize, barley, and sugar cane, cover 46% of the world's farmland — what group of plants is this?
Grass: Collective name for three families of plants.
This British mathematician has studied the math of dating and pandemics, delivered the Royal Institution's 2019 Christmas Lectures, and hosted BBC's 'Secret Genius of Modern Life' — who is she?
Hannah Fry: British mathematician and broadcaster (born 1984)
Its name Greek for 'different wings,' this insect suborder of about 40,000 species is the group most consistently termed 'true bugs' within Hemiptera — which group is it?
Heteroptera: Suborder of true bugs. The name "Heteroptera" is used in two very different ways in modern classifications.
Also known as dihydrocodeinone, this semi-synthetic opioid is often combined with acetaminophen or ibuprofen for pain and is sold alone as an extended-release drug called Zohydro ER — what is it?
Hydrocodone: Opioid drug used in pain relief.

Named after both a biblical sea monster and the author of 'Moby-Dick,' this extinct predatory sperm whale roamed ancient oceans roughly 9 million years ago — which genus?
Livyatan: Extinct genus of sperm whale from the Miocene epoch.
Native to northeastern Australia and first commercially grown at scale in Hawaii during the 1880s, this is the only widely cultivated food plant indigenous to Australia — what nut is it?

Kangaroos, koalas, and wombats all belong to this mammal group whose young are born undeveloped and finish developing in their mother's pouch — what group is it?
Marsupial: Infraclass of mammals in the clade Metatheria.

Nelumbo nucifera: Species of aquatic flowering plant. It is sometimes colloquially called a water lily, though this more often refers to members of the family Nymphaeaceae.

Parrot: Order of birds. One-third of all parrot species are threatened by extinction, with a higher aggregate extinction risk (IUCN Red List Index) than any other comparable bird group.
Secreted by eccrine and apocrine glands, this bodily fluid can flow at up to 4 litres per hour in adults and cools the body via evaporation — what is it?
Perspiration: Fluid secreted from sudoriferous glands.
This scientific term covers walruses, sea lions, and true seals — fin-footed marine mammals whose closest living relatives are weasels and raccoons — what is the term?
Pinniped: Taxonomic group of semi-aquatic mammals.

A colorless salt that looks unnervingly like sugar but tastes acrid and bitter, this compound is mostly used in gold mining and electroplating — and just 200 to 300 milligrams will kill nearly any human. What is it?
Potassium cyanide: Chemical compound. It is a colorless salt, similar in appearance to sugar, that is highly soluble in water.

This deep-sea fish off Australia and New Zealand has almost no muscle and a gelatinous body just under water's density, letting it float effortlessly at depths beyond 600 meters — what is its scientific name?
Psychrolutes marcidus: Species of fish. Psychrolutes marcidus, the smooth-head blobfish, or simply the blobfish, is a deep-sea fish of the family Psychrolutidae.

In this rare congenital condition affecting about 1 in 10,000 people, the heart and other major organs sit as a mirror image of their normal position — what's it called?
Situs inversus: Condition in which organs are reversed.

Encased by the vertebral column and running from the brainstem down to about the first lumbar vertebra, this hollow, fluid-filled structure forms the other half of the central nervous system alongside the brain — what is it?
Spinal cord: Part of the vertebral column in animals.

Native to New Guinea and domesticated by Papuan and Austronesian peoples, this tall grass with sucrose-rich stalks was carried across the Pacific and eventually to India and China in ancient times. What crop is it?
Sugarcane: Several species of grass used for sugar production.
Also known as estragon, this perennial herb in the daisy family comes in a French variety prized for cooking and a milder Russian variety — which herb?
Tarragon: Species of flowering plant in the daisy family Asteraceae.
The body's primary muscle of respiration, this dome-shaped sheet separates the chest cavity from the abdomen and contracts to pull air into the lungs — what is it?

This medical condition occurs when kidney failure allows urea and other metabolic waste products to build up dangerously in the bloodstream. What's it called?

Named for the French word for 'watcher,' this paraphilia involves secretly observing strangers in private, intimate moments and gave rise to the nickname 'Peeping Tom' — what is it called?
Voyeurism: Sexual interest in or practice of spying on people engaged in intimate behaviors.

Wound healing: Series of events that restore integrity to damaged tissue after an injury.
